content: Histidine triad nucleotide-binding protein 2 (HINT2) is a mitochondrial protein encoded by the HINT2 gene located on chromosome 9 in humans. This protein functions as an AMP-lysine hydrolase and phosphoamidase, and it is believed to play a role in tumor suppression. HINT2 belongs to the histidine triad nucleotide-binding (Hint) protein family, which is a subfamily of the histidine triad (HIT) protein family. It contains a conserved histidine and a HIT sequence motif (His-X-His-X-His-X-X), where the last two histidines form part of a catalytic triad. The protein consists of 163 amino acids and forms a 17-kDa homodimer. When compared to other Hint family members, HINT2 shares 61% sequence homology with HINT1 and 28% sequence homology with HINT3. Notably, HINT2 has a 35-amino acid extension at its N-terminal, which is predicted to function as a mitochondrial import signal, distinguishing it from HINT1. HINT2 is a member of the HIT superfamily and the Hint subfamily, which are characterized as nucleotide hydrolases and transferases that act on the alpha-phosphate of ribonucleotides. The Hint family is the most ancient within the HIT superfamily, and its members are highly conserved across eukaryotes and archaebacteria. Hint proteins, including HINT2, function as AMP-lysine hydrolases and phosphoramidases. In mammals, HINT2 is expressed in the liver, adrenal cortex, and pancreas, where it localizes to the mitochondria. Specifically, it is situated in the inner mitochondrial membrane, facing the mitochondrial matrix. This localization is thought to facilitate the transport of cholesterol from the cytosol to the mitochondrial matrix, a process essential for steroidogenesis. HINT2 likely provides a contact site for cholesterol, enabling it to traverse the mitochondrial intermembrane space. HINT2 regulates steroidogenesis through both calcium-dependent and calcium-independent signaling pathways, which may help maintain optimal mitochondrial membrane potential. Its role in calcium homeostasis is also thought to contribute to its pro-apoptotic function in hepatocytes and other non-steroidogenic cells, although the precise mechanisms remain unclear. HINT2 is one of three members of the Hint protein family and is exclusively localized to mitochondria in various cell types. In human adrenocarcinoma cells, HINT2 modulates mitochondrial calcium (Ca2+) handling. Intracellular calcium plays a critical role in numerous physiological processes across all living organisms. Extracellular stimuli generate temporally organized Ca2+ signals, often in the form of repetitive spikes. The frequency of these oscillations determines the nature and extent of the cellular response. These oscillations arise from the repetitive opening of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (InsP3) receptors, which are Ca2+ channels embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. The opening of these channels is triggered by a stimulus-induced increase in InsP3 levels. Since the activity of these receptors is biphasically regulated by cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels, oscillations can occur. Mitochondria also influence cytoplasmic Ca2+ signals by buffering cytosolic Ca2+ changes and releasing Ca2+. At rest, the intramitochondrial and cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations are similar, approximately 100 nM. The Hint protein family, including HINT2, has been implicated in tumor suppression. HINT2, specifically, is localized to mitochondria near the contact sites of the inner membrane. It is highly expressed in the liver, where it has been shown to enhance mitochondrial lipid metabolism, respiration, and glucose homeostasis. HINT2 modulates both cytoplasmic and mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics by stimulating the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. The absence of HINT2 has been associated with premature opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) in mitochondrial suspensions. Consequently, HINT2 plays a significant role in mitochondrial cell death signaling, such as apoptosis, and in ischemia-reperfusion injury, as seen during heart attacks, through its regulation of calcium homeostasis. HINT2 expression patterns vary in different cancers. It is upregulated in breast, pancreatic, and colon cancer cells, while it is downregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma and endometrial cancer. Although its exact role in tumor suppression remains unclear, studies suggest that HINT2 may promote apoptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma and endometrial cancer. In double knockout Hint2 mice, increased acylation and morphological changes were observed in mitochondria, indicating that HINT2 may regulate glucose and lipid metabolism. Currently, no protein-protein interaction partners have been identified for HINT2.
